issues.legal_issue: The duty to consider a borrower’s representation and communicate reasons for rejecting it is mandatory.
material_facts: After receiving a demand notice, the borrower sent the creditor a representation proposing rescheduling of the loan.
The creditor did not send a written response stating reasons for rejecting the representation.
issues.conclusion: The creditor must actively consider a borrower’s representation or objection and, if it rejects it as unacceptable or untenable, communicate its reasons within the prescribed time; this requirement is mandatory.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(3A) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, read with Rule 3A of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, requires consideration and a reasoned communication when a representation is rejected. The imperative language and the provision’s purpose of giving the creditor a pause to reconsider make the duty mandatory. The Court relied on Mardia Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India, Transcore v. Union of India, Keshavlal Khemchand & Sons (P) Ltd. v. Union of India, and the principles of statutory construction discussed in State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya and other cited decisions.

predicates.secured_creditor_receives_borrower_repre: A borrower makes a representation or objection after a secured creditor sends a demand notice.
predicates.secured_creditor_rejects_representation: The secured creditor decides not to accept the borrower’s representation.
predicates.secured_creditor_finds_representation_un: The secured creditor concludes that the borrower’s representation is untenable.

issues.definition: When a secured creditor receives a borrower’s representation and rejects it or considers it untenable, the creditor must consider it and communicate reasons for the rejection.

issues.legal_issue: A breach of the mandatory duty to respond to a representation does not necessarily entitle a borrower to discretionary equitable relief when the creditor has in substance considered the proposals and the borrower has repeatedly failed to meet repayment commitments.
material_facts: The borrower’s representation sought more time and rescheduling of repayment.
The creditor negotiated with the borrower, deferred a sale, and granted opportunities and additional time to repay.
The borrower sent cheques that were dishonoured, made further unfulfilled repayment proposals, and gave an undertaking acknowledging the creditor’s right to sell the assets upon default.
The debt remained unpaid and undisputed, and the creditor considered the repayment proposals during the negotiations despite not sending a written response to the original representation.
The borrower sought relief in constitutional proceedings challenging enforcement and sale of the secured assets.
issues.conclusion: Although the creditor did not reply in writing, the borrower was not entitled to discretionary equitable relief because the creditor had considered the repayment proposals and the borrower’s conduct consisted of repeated requests for time followed by non-payment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the duty under Section 13(3A) as mandatory but held that the construction of the Act is not altered by the facts of an individual case and that relief in discretionary proceedings may be refused where the claimant’s conduct warrants refusal. Under Articles 226 and 136 of the Constitution, equitable relief depends on unblameworthy conduct. The Court relied on State of Maharashtra v. Digambar and Lindsay Petroleum Co. v. Hurd, including the relevance of delay and acts done during the interval.

predicates.borrower_seeks_discretionary_constitutio: A borrower asks a court exercising discretionary constitutional jurisdiction to restrain or invalidate enforcement of secured assets.
predicates.secured_creditor_considered_repayment_pr: The creditor considered the borrower’s repayment proposals during negotiations and gave opportunities to repay.
predicates.borrower_repeatedly_failed_to_repay_as_p: The borrower repeatedly promised repayment or sought more time but did not meet the resulting commitments.
predicates.debt_remains_undisputed: The borrower does not dispute the underlying debt or liability.

issues.definition: A borrower seeking discretionary constitutional relief is not entitled to that relief when the creditor considered repayment proposals, the borrower repeatedly failed to repay as promised, and the debt remains undisputed.

issues.legal_issue: A debtor’s written acknowledgment of an undisputed debt is not deprived of effect merely because it is marked “without prejudice” or made during negotiations.
material_facts: During negotiations, the borrower gave a written undertaking accepting a repayment schedule and acknowledging the creditor’s right to sell the secured assets if the borrower defaulted.
The letter was marked “without prejudice.”
The debt remained unpaid and undisputed.
issues.conclusion: The words “without prejudice” did not deprive the undertaking of significance; the letter acknowledged the debt and the creditor’s right to proceed upon default.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Spencer v. Hemmerde and Bradford and Bingley v. Rashid. It explained that where a statement is relied on as an acknowledgment for the purpose of the applicable acknowledgment rule, it is the acknowledgment itself, not evidence of some separate admission, and the “without prejudice” rule does not prevent its use in that way.

predicates.debtor_makes_written_debt_acknowledgment: A debtor makes a written statement during negotiations acknowledging an unpaid debt or the creditor’s rights upon default.
predicates.letter_marked_without_prejudice: The written statement is marked “without prejudice.”
predicates.debt_remains_unpaid: The acknowledged debt has not been paid.

issues.definition: A written acknowledgment made during negotiations remains an acknowledgment despite a “without prejudice” marking when the debt is unpaid.

issues.legal_issue: Land is not agricultural land merely because it is recorded as agricultural or can support some cultivation; its actual condition, intended use, and connection with an agricultural purpose determine its character.
material_facts: The mortgaged parcels were part of the single property used for a hotel and were mortgaged as part of that hotel property.
The borrower had applied to convert the parcels from agricultural to non-agricultural use, but the application remained pending.
A relatively small part of the total property was used to grow produce and trees for the hotel’s captive consumption, and the evidence of substantial cultivation was limited.
The parcels were recorded as agricultural land in revenue records and had been purchased from agriculturists.
issues.conclusion: The land was not agricultural land for the purpose of the statutory exemption because its character and intended use connected it with the hotel, not with an agricultural purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31(i) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, excludes security interests created in agricultural land from the Act. The character of land depends on its actual condition and intended use and its connection with an agricultural purpose, not merely on its potential for cultivation or revenue entries. The Court relied on Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Andhra Pradesh v. Officer-in-Charge (Court of Wards), Paigah and Kunjukutty Saheb v. State of Kerala.

predicates.security_covers_land_used_as_part_of_non: The secured land forms part of a property held and used for a non-agricultural purpose.
predicates.land_has_no_substantial_agricultural_use: The land is not in substantial actual use for agriculture.
predicates.cultivation_is_incidental_to_nonagricult: Any growing of produce or trees is incidental to the non-agricultural use of the property.

issues.definition: Land forming part of a non-agricultural property, without substantial agricultural use and with only incidental cultivation, is not agricultural for the exemption.

issues.legal_issue: The exemption for security interests in agricultural land is within Parliament’s legislative competence because it forms part of legislation concerning banking and debt recovery rather than legislation on land.
material_facts: The borrower challenged Parliament’s competence to enact the provision excluding security interests in agricultural land from the Act.
The provision addressed whether the Act’s debt-recovery mechanism applied to security interests over agricultural land.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to legislative competence failed; the provision was within Parliament’s competence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that Section 31(i) concerns the scope of a law governing security interests and debt recovery, not legislation on agricultural land itself. It relied on Entry 45 of List I and on Union of India v. Delhi High Court Bar Association, which treated banking recovery mechanisms as within Parliament’s competence, and State Bank of India v. Santosh Gupta, which referred to Entries 45 and 95 of List I. The Court also relied on A.S. Krishna v. State of Madras concerning the proper approach to assessing a statute as an organic whole.

predicates.challenge_concerns_parliamentary_power_o: A party challenges Parliament’s competence to enact a provision governing recovery of secured debts.
predicates.challenged_provision_defines_scope_of_se: The challenged provision defines when a debt-recovery enforcement mechanism may be used for security interests.

issues.definition: A provision defining the scope of secured-debt enforcement falls within Parliament’s competence when the challenge concerns its power to legislate on debt recovery.

issues.legal_issue: Symbolic possession may support a sale of secured assets, and a secured creditor that has transferred only a limited interest while retaining the right to take actual possession remains a secured creditor entitled to seek assistance in obtaining possession.
material_facts: The creditor took symbolic rather than actual possession of the secured property before the auction.
The debtor continued to occupy and operate the property after symbolic possession was taken.
The creditor sold the property at auction and issued a sale certificate to the purchaser.
The creditor sought assistance to obtain physical possession after the sale.
The creditor had not transferred actual possession to the purchaser and retained the right to obtain it.
issues.conclusion: Symbolic possession was not illegal; the creditor remained a secured creditor after the limited transfer and could seek an order for physical possession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found nothing in the Act making symbolic possession illegal and relied on M.V.S. Manikayala Rao v. M.Narasimhaswami concerning the legal significance of symbolic possession. Under Section 2(d), a secured creditor includes the relevant creditor holding an interest in the security; Section 13(6) vests in a transferee the rights transferred as if the transfer had been made by the owner. Because actual possession and the associated interest had not passed to the creditor or the purchaser, the creditor remained a secured creditor with the right to obtain actual possession and could apply under Section 14.

predicates.secured_asset_enforcement_involves_aucti: A secured creditor enforces a security interest by auctioning the secured asset.
predicates.creditor_took_symbolic_possession_before: The creditor took symbolic or constructive possession of the asset before the sale.
predicates.debtor_retained_actual_possession: The debtor continued to hold actual possession after symbolic possession was taken.
predicates.creditor_retained_right_to_obtain_actual: The creditor retained an interest in the asset that included the right to obtain actual possession.

issues.definition: In an enforcement auction, symbolic possession is permissible and the creditor may seek actual possession if the debtor retains possession and the creditor retains the right to obtain it.

issues.legal_issue: An inference of fraud or collusion in an auction sale cannot be based merely on the purchaser’s awareness of a pending dispute or on an asserted irregularity unsupported by evidence of manipulation.
material_facts: The property was sold after a fourth publicly advertised auction, following earlier auctions that did not produce a sale.
The auction purchaser knew that a dispute was pending but bid for the property.
The purchaser paid the full sale consideration.

The High Court relied in part on the purchaser’s awareness of the dispute and on a statement about when the sale would be confirmed, but the record did not establish what had occurred after the stated time.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances did not support the High Court’s finding of fraud or collusion; the auction sale was not shown to have been manipulated or collusive.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a purchaser’s willingness to take the risk of buying disputed immovable property does not itself establish collusion. It also found that the lack of evidence about what occurred after the stated time prevented an inference of manipulation, particularly where the sale followed public advertising and the consideration was paid in full.

predicates.property_is_sold_in_publicly_advertised_: The property is sold through a publicly advertised auction.
predicates.purchaser_pays_full_consideration: The purchaser pays the entire auction consideration.
predicates.fraud_inference_rests_only_on_purchaser_: The alleged fraud or collusion is inferred only from the purchaser’s awareness of a pending dispute.
predicates.no_evidence_of_manipulation: The record contains no evidence establishing manipulation of the sale.

issues.definition: A publicly advertised auction sale for which full consideration is paid is not shown to be fraudulent or collusive when the inference rests only on the purchaser’s knowledge of a dispute and there is no evidence of manipulation.
